questions.question: What is ZooKeeper's primary role in a distributed system?
options: Store large application records and analytical datasets
Coordinate small pieces of shared state such as membership, ownership, and configuration
Replace every service-to-service message broker
Serve as a high-throughput object store
questions.explanation: ZooKeeper is a coordination service. It keeps small, strongly ordered metadata that helps participants agree on ownership, membership, naming, and configuration.

questions.question: How many acknowledgements form a write quorum in a five-voter ensemble?
questions.explanation: A quorum is a strict majority: floor(5 / 2) + 1 = 3. Any two voters can be unavailable while three remain able to make progress.

questions.question: Why does a four-voter ensemble usually provide no failure-tolerance benefit over three voters?
options: Four voters require three acknowledgements, so losing two still stops progress
ZooKeeper refuses to start any even-sized ensemble
The fourth voter stores no replicated state
Four voters require all four acknowledgements
questions.explanation: Both three and four voters tolerate only one failed voter. Four voters require a quorum of three, so the extra voter adds replication work without increasing the number of tolerated failures.

questions.question: A five-voter ensemble is split 3-2 across two zones. What happens if the three-voter zone fails?
options: The remaining two voters elect a leader and continue writes
Reads and writes continue because five voters tolerate any zone failure
The remaining two voters cannot form the required quorum of three
The failed voters automatically become observers
questions.explanation: Failure tolerance depends on placement as well as voter count. Losing the zone that holds the majority leaves only two voters, which cannot form a five-member ensemble's quorum of three.

questions.question: What happens to an ephemeral znode after its owning ZooKeeper session expires?
options: It becomes persistent
It remains until an operator deletes it
It moves to the next client session automatically
ZooKeeper removes it, allowing other participants to observe the lost owner
questions.explanation: Ephemeral znodes are bound to a session. Expiration permanently ends that session and removes its ephemeral state.

questions.question: Why should a watch handler reread the znode instead of treating each notification as a complete change record?
options: A watch signals that state may have changed and multiple mutations can be represented by one notification
Watch notifications contain the entire ZooKeeper transaction log
A watch always arrives before the corresponding write
Rereading converts an ephemeral znode into a persistent one
questions.explanation: A watch is an invalidation signal, not an event stream. The safe pattern is to fetch the current version and establish the next watch, then derive behavior from that authoritative state.

questions.question: Why does a leader often need a fencing token in addition to an ephemeral election node?
options: The token compresses znode payloads
An old leader can remain paused or disconnected and later try to write to an external resource
The token increases the ZooKeeper session timeout
The token makes watches persistent across all client libraries
questions.explanation: A monotonically increasing fencing token lets the protected resource reject work from an older leader, even if that process resumes after another participant has taken ownership.

questions.question: Which workload is the poorest fit for ZooKeeper?
options: Publishing a small service-membership directory
Choosing one leader from several candidates
Storing large user documents and serving ad hoc analytical queries
Coordinating a versioned configuration pointer
questions.explanation: Large records, scans, and analytical queries belong in a database or object store. ZooKeeper should hold only the small coordination state needed to locate or govern that data.
